value.body: Pharmaceutical plants employ pharmacy graduates in three linked functions: production (running and documenting manufacturing batches), quality control (testing raw materials and finished products in the lab) and quality assurance (making sure processes, records and audits meet Good Manufacturing Practice). It is one of the largest entry points for B.Pharm graduates.

items.label: GMP standard
items.note: Drugs Rules, 1945; revised schedule notified December 2023

items.label: Regulators
items.note: Export plants are also inspected by foreign regulators

items.label: Approved technical staff
items.note: Manufacturing and testing licences name qualified, approved staff; a pharmacy degree is one accepted qualification

items.label: Pharma exports
items.note: Drugs and pharmaceuticals; about 9% higher than the year before

items.label: B.Pharm pass-outs a year
items.note: Not all go into manufacturing; retail, hospital, sales and higher study also absorb graduates
items.source: AISHE 2023-24 (Ministry of Education), institutions that reported

value.title: How you get in
value.body: A B.Pharm (or D.Pharm/M.Pharm, or a science degree for some QC roles). Hiring is direct — campus placement, walk-in drives or applications to plants. There is no entrance exam; companies may test basic pharmaceutics, analytical chemistry and GMP knowledge.

value.title: At a glance
items: Plants are concentrated in industrial clusters, so relocation is common.
Production and QC often involve shift work and strict documentation.
Experience with audits, analytical instruments (HPLC, GC) and data-integrity practices helps movement into QA, regulatory affairs or validation.
Entry pay is modest; growth depends on the plant's scale and regulatory exposure.

value.title: B.Pharm enrolment (regular mode)
value.note: Students across all years of the course in regular mode. Enrolment roughly doubled in five years; this reflects more colleges and seats, not more plant jobs.
